lessons.title: More Input Types
lessons.content: HTML5 introduced many new input types that provide better user experiences, especially on mobile devices, by showing custom keyboards or widgets.

lessons.title: Date and Time Inputs
lessons.content: Use `<input type='date'>`, `<input type='time'>`, and `<input type='datetime-local'>` to allow users to easily select dates and times from a native UI.

lessons.title: Create an input field for a user to select their birthday.

lessons.question: Which input type is best for picking a flight departure time?

lessons.title: Specialized Inputs
lessons.content: Types like `<input type='color'>` shows a color picker, `<input type='range'>` creates a slider, and `<input type='file'>` allows file uploads.

lessons.title: Create a volume control slider from 0 to 100.

lessons.question: Which input type would you use to let a user upload a profile picture?

lessons.instruction: Create an input for entering an email address.

lessons.title: Input Innovator! 💡
lessons.content: You've expanded your form toolkit! Using these specialized inputs makes your forms more user-friendly and robust.

lessons.title: The `<label>` Element
lessons.content: The `<label>` element is crucial for accessibility. It links a text description to a form control. Clicking the label focuses the input.

lessons.title: Linking Labels
lessons.content: You link a `<label>` to an `<input>` by giving the input an `id` and matching it with the label's `for` attribute.

lessons.title: Create a text input with a properly linked label for 'Username'.

lessons.question: Which two attributes connect a label and an input?

lessons.title: Grouping with `<fieldset>`
lessons.content: The `<fieldset>` element groups related controls within a form. The `<legend>` element provides a caption for the fieldset.

lessons.title: Group 'name' and 'email' inputs inside a fieldset with the legend 'User Details'.

lessons.question: What is the purpose of `<fieldset>`?

lessons.title: The `placeholder` Attribute
lessons.content: The `placeholder` attribute provides a short hint (like a sample value or format) that appears in the input field before the user enters a value.

lessons.instruction: Add a placeholder to the input.

lessons.title: Form Architect! 🏛️
lessons.content: Your forms are now not only functional but also well-structured and accessible. This is a mark of a professional developer.

lessons.title: Browser-Based Validation
lessons.content: HTML5 provides attributes that let the browser validate form fields without any JavaScript, providing instant feedback to the user.

lessons.title: The `required` Attribute
lessons.content: The boolean attribute `required` specifies that an input field must be filled out before the form can be submitted.

lessons.title: Make an email input field mandatory.

lessons.question: What does the `required` attribute do?

lessons.title: Restricting Length
lessons.content: Use `minlength` and `maxlength` to specify the minimum and maximum number of characters allowed in a text-based input.

lessons.title: Create a password input that must be at least 8 characters long.
Pattern Matching
lessons.content: The `pattern` attribute takes a Regular Expression, allowing you to define a specific format the input value must match (e.g., a postal code).

lessons.title: Create an input that only accepts 3-digit numbers.
Validation Vanguard! 🛡️
lessons.content: You can now build self-validating forms right in your HTML, improving data quality and user experience with zero JavaScript.

lessons.title: Dropdown Lists
lessons.content: For a long list of choices, a dropdown menu is better than radio buttons. This is created with the `<select>` and `<option>` tags.

lessons.title: The `<select>` and `<option>` Tags
lessons.content: The `<select>` tag is the container. Each `<option>` tag inside it represents one choice in the list. The `value` attribute of the option is what gets submitted.

lessons.title: Create a dropdown to select a country.

lessons.question: Which tag defines an item in a dropdown list?

lessons.title: Grouping Options
lessons.content: You can group related options together within a `<select>` list using the `<optgroup>` tag, which takes a `label` attribute for the group name.

lessons.title: Create a dropdown with grouped options for 'Fruits' and 'Vegetables'.
Multi-line Text Input
lessons.content: For long-form user input, like comments or messages, the `<textarea>` element is the correct choice instead of a single-line `<input>`.

lessons.title: Create a text area for user comments.

lessons.instruction: Create an option with the value 'de' for Germany.

lessons.title: Selection Specialist! 🎯
lessons.content: You've mastered more advanced form controls, allowing you to gather complex and varied user input with ease.

lessons.title: Semantic Tables
lessons.content: For large data tables, it's important to structure them semantically. This helps browsers, assistive technologies, and even search engines understand your data.

lessons.title: Header, Body, and Footer
lessons.content: You can group your table content into `<thead>` for the header row(s), `<tbody>` for the main data rows, and `<tfoot>` for the footer row(s).

lessons.title: Create a table with a `<thead>` and a `<tbody>` section.

lessons.question: Which tag is used for the main data rows of a table?

lessons.title: The `<caption>` Element
lessons.content: The `<caption>` tag provides a title or description for the entire table. It should be the first child of the `<table>` element and is crucial for accessibility.

lessons.title: Add a caption 'Monthly Sales Figures' to a table.
Column Groups
lessons.content: The `<colgroup>` and `<col>` elements allow you to group and style entire columns at once, without adding classes to every single cell.

lessons.title: Define a table with two columns using `<colgroup>`.

lessons.instruction: Add the `<tfoot>` element to wrap the summary row.

lessons.title: Table Tactician! 📊
lessons.content: You can now structure large data tables in a way that is semantic, accessible, and easy to style. This is a vital skill for displaying complex data.

lessons.title: Merging Cells
lessons.content: Sometimes, a data cell needs to span across multiple columns or rows. HTML provides attributes for this purpose.

lessons.title: Spanning Columns
lessons.content: The `colspan` attribute is used on a `<th>` or `<td>` to make it span across more than one column.

lessons.title: Create a header cell that spans two columns.

lessons.question: What does `colspan='3'` do?

lessons.title: Spanning Rows
lessons.content: Similarly, the `rowspan` attribute is used on a `<th>` or `<td>` to make it span across more than one row.

lessons.title: Create a data cell that spans two rows.

lessons.question: Which attribute makes a cell taller, spanning multiple rows?

lessons.instruction: Make the header cell span 3 columns.

lessons.title: Create a complex cell that spans 2 columns and 2 rows.
Table Architect! 🏗️
lessons.content: You've mastered the art of creating complex table layouts. This allows for sophisticated data presentation far beyond simple grids.

lessons.title: More Media Control
lessons.content: The `<audio>` and `<video>` tags have several attributes to give you more control over how media is presented and played.

lessons.title: Video Attributes
lessons.content: Use `autoplay` to start the video automatically (often requires `muted`), `loop` to repeat it, and `poster` to show an image before the video loads.

lessons.title: Create a video that loops and shows a poster image.

lessons.question: Which attribute shows an image before a video plays?

lessons.title: Multiple Sources
lessons.content: Different browsers support different video/audio formats. You can provide multiple formats inside a `<video>` or `<audio>` tag using the `<source>` element.

lessons.title: Provide both MP4 and WebM video formats.
Subtitles and Captions
lessons.content: The `<track>` element is used to specify timed text tracks, such as subtitles or captions. This is essential for accessibility.

lessons.title: Add an English subtitles track to a video.
lessons.expectedAnswer:
<video src='movie.mp4' controls>
  <track src='subs_en.vtt' kind='subtitles' srclang='en' label='English'>
</video>
blocks:
<video src='movie.mp4' controls>
  <track src='subs_en.vtt' kind='subtitles' srclang='en' label='English'>
</video>

lessons.instruction: Add the `loop` attribute to make the audio repeat.

lessons.title: Multimedia Maestro! 🎬
lessons.content: You can now embed and control multimedia like a pro, ensuring it's accessible and compatible across different browsers.

lessons.title: Images for Every Screen
lessons.content: On modern websites, it's inefficient to serve a huge desktop image to a small mobile phone. HTML provides ways to serve different images based on screen size.

lessons.title: The `srcset` Attribute
lessons.content: The `srcset` attribute on an `` tag allows you to provide a comma-separated list of image files and their inherent widths.

lessons.title: Provide small and large versions of a banner image using `srcset`.

lessons.question: What does the 'w' unit in `srcset` describe?
options: The image's inherent width in pixels
lessons.correct: The image's inherent width in pixels

lessons.title: The `<picture>` Element
lessons.content: For more advanced control, like serving completely different image formats (e.g., modern WebP vs. older JPG), you can use the `<picture>` element.

lessons.title: `<picture>` and `<source>`
lessons.content: Inside ``, you list `` elements with different `srcset` and `type` attributes. The browser picks the first one it supports. The final `` is a fallback.

lessons.title: Use `<picture>` to provide a WebP image with a JPG fallback.

lessons.question: Inside a `` element, what is the purpose of the `` tag?
options: It's a fallback for older browsers
lessons.correct: It's a fallback for older browsers

lessons.instruction: Add a `<source>` element inside the `<picture>` container.

lessons.title: Image Optimizer! 🖼️
lessons.content: You've learned how to make your websites faster and more efficient by serving the right image for the right device. This is a critical modern web skill.

lessons.title: Beyond the `<div>`
lessons.content: While `<div>` is a generic container, HTML5 introduced semantic layout elements that describe their purpose, improving accessibility and SEO.

lessons.title: The `<header>` Element
lessons.content: The `<header>` element represents introductory content, typically a group of introductory or navigational aids. It can be for the whole page or for a section.

lessons.title: Create a page header containing a logo and the main heading.
The `<footer>` Element
lessons.content: The `<footer>` element represents the footer for its nearest sectioning ancestor. It typically contains copyright information, contact details, or related links.

lessons.title: Create a page footer with a copyright notice.
The `<nav>` Element
lessons.content: The `<nav>` element is specifically for major navigation blocks, such as the main site menu.

lessons.title: Create a navigation menu using `<nav>` and an unordered list.
The `<main>` Element
lessons.content: The `<main>` element represents the dominant, unique content of the `<body>`. There should only be one `<main>` element per page.

lessons.question: Which semantic element is for the primary content of the page?

lessons.title: Layout Luminary! ✨
lessons.content: You now understand how to structure the main layout of a page semantically, making your sites more meaningful to browsers and screen readers.

lessons.title: Structuring Content Blocks
lessons.content: Inside your `<main>` element, you can further structure your content with more specific semantic tags.

lessons.title: The `<section>` Element
lessons.content: The `<section>` element represents a standalone thematic grouping of content. It should almost always have a heading.

lessons.title: Create a 'Contact Us' section with a heading and a paragraph.
The `<article>` Element
lessons.content: The `<article>` element represents a self-contained composition that is independently distributable or reusable, like a blog post, forum post, or news story.

lessons.question: Which tag is best for a single blog post on a page of many posts?

lessons.title: Mark up a short news story using `<article>`.
The `<aside>` Element
lessons.content: The `<aside>` element represents content that is tangentially related to the main content around it, such as a sidebar, pull quotes, or ad groups.

lessons.title: Create a sidebar with related links.

lessons.question: Which element would you use for a glossary definition in a sidebar?

lessons.title: Content Connoisseur! 🧐
lessons.content: You can now structure not just the page layout, but the content itself, with a high degree of semantic precision. This is a top-tier HTML skill.

lessons.title: What is Accessibility?
lessons.content: Web accessibility (often abbreviated A11y) is the practice of making websites usable by as many people as possible, including those with disabilities.

lessons.title: Why is it Important?
lessons.content: It's not only the right thing to do, but it also improves the experience for all users, boosts SEO, and is a legal requirement in many places.

lessons.question: Who benefits from web accessibility?

lessons.title: Semantic HTML is Key
lessons.content: The single most important thing you can do for accessibility is to use semantic HTML correctly. A screen reader uses tags like `<nav>` and `<h1>` to help users navigate.

lessons.question: What is the most fundamental practice for good A11y?

lessons.title: The `alt` Attribute Revisited
lessons.content: We've seen `alt` on `` tags. This alternative text is what a screen reader will announce to a visually impaired user. It's not optional, it's essential.

lessons.title: Write an image tag with descriptive alt text.
Link Text
lessons.content: Avoid generic link text like 'Click Here'. The link text should be descriptive of where the link will take the user, e.g., 'Read our full privacy policy'.

lessons.question: Which is better link text?

lessons.title: A11y Advocate! ❤️
lessons.content: You've taken the first step toward building a more inclusive web. Thinking about accessibility from the start will make you a better developer.

lessons.title: What is ARIA?
lessons.content: ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) is a set of attributes you can add to HTML to make web content more accessible, especially for dynamic JavaScript widgets.

lessons.title: When to Use ARIA
lessons.content: Rule #1 of ARIA: Don't use ARIA if you can use a native semantic HTML element instead. For example, use a `<button>` tag instead of `<div role='button'>`.

lessons.question: Which is better for accessibility?

lessons.title: The `role` Attribute
lessons.content: The `role` attribute can define a role for an element that it doesn't have natively, like `role='alert'` for a status message `<div>`.

lessons.title: Give a `<div>` the role of a navigation menu.
State Attributes
lessons.content: ARIA attributes like `aria-label`, `aria-hidden`, and `aria-expanded` can provide more information about the state of an element.

lessons.title: Add an ARIA label to a close button that only has an 'X' icon.

lessons.question: What does `aria-hidden='true'` do?
options: Hides the element from screen readers
lessons.correct: Hides the element from screen readers

lessons.instruction: Add a `role` attribute to the search box div.

lessons.title: Accessibility Ally! 🤝
lessons.content: You've learned the basics of ARIA. This powerful tool helps you bridge the accessibility gaps in complex web applications. Use it wisely!

lessons.title: A Window to Another Page
lessons.content: An `<iframe>` (Inline Frame) is used to embed another HTML document within the current one. It's commonly used for maps, videos, or payment gateways.

lessons.title: Basic Syntax
lessons.content: The `src` attribute specifies the URL of the page to embed. `width` and `height` attributes control the size of the frame.

lessons.title: Embed an example website in an iframe.

lessons.question: Which attribute defines the address of the page to embed?

lessons.title: The `title` Attribute
lessons.content: For accessibility, it's very important to add a `title` attribute to your `<iframe>` to describe what it contains for screen reader users.

lessons.title: Embed a YouTube video with a descriptive title.
lessons.expectedAnswer: <iframe src='...' title='YouTube video player for Learning HTML'></iframe>
blocks: <iframe src='...' title='YouTube video player for Learning HTML'></iframe>

lessons.title: Security with `sandbox`
lessons.content: If you're embedding untrusted content, the `sandbox` attribute lets you restrict what the embedded page can do, like run scripts or submit forms.

lessons.question: What is the purpose of the `sandbox` attribute?

lessons.instruction: Add a `height` attribute to the iframe.

lessons.title: Content Curator! 큐
lessons.content: You can now embed third-party content seamlessly and securely into your web pages, a common requirement in modern web development.

lessons.title: Reserved Characters
lessons.content: Some characters are reserved in HTML, like `<` and `>`. If you want to display them as text, you need to use character entities.

lessons.title: Common Entities
lessons.content: The most common entities are `<` for <, `>` for >, and `&` for &.

lessons.title:
Display the text '

' literally on the page.

lessons.question: Which entity represents the less-than sign (<)?

lessons.title: Non-Breaking Space
lessons.content: The ` ` entity is a non-breaking space. It prevents an automatic line break from happening at its position.

lessons.title: Ensure '10 USD' always stays on the same line.
Symbol Entities
lessons.content: Entities are also used for symbols that aren't on a standard keyboard, like `©` for the copyright symbol © or `®` for ®.

lessons.title: Add a copyright symbol to your footer.
Symbol Sage! ™️
lessons.content: You've learned how to handle special characters and symbols correctly, ensuring your content always displays as intended.

lessons.title: Native Interactivity
lessons.content: HTML5 provides some elements that have built-in interactivity, working out of the box with no JavaScript required.

lessons.title: The `<details>` Element
lessons.content: The `<details>` element creates a disclosure widget in which information is visible only when the widget is toggled into an 'open' state.

lessons.title: The `<summary>` Element
lessons.content: A `<summary>` tag is used inside `<details>` to provide a visible heading for the hidden content. Clicking the summary toggles the view.

lessons.title: Create a simple show/hide widget using `<details>` and `<summary>`.

lessons.question: What is the role of the `<summary>` tag?
options: It's the always-visible title for a `<details>` widget
lessons.correct: It's the always-visible title for a `<details>` widget

lessons.title: Datalists for Autocomplete
lessons.content: The `<datalist>` element provides an 'autocomplete' feature for `<input>` elements. It contains a set of `<option>`s that will be suggested to the user.

lessons.title: Create a text input with a datalist of suggested browser names.

lessons.question: How do you link an `<input>` to a `<datalist>`?

lessons.instruction: Add a `<summary>` to the details widget.

lessons.title: Interaction Inventor! 🪄
lessons.content: You can now build some common interactive patterns using only HTML, making your sites more engaging and user-friendly with less code.

lessons.title: Semantic Captions
lessons.content: Sometimes, an image, diagram, or code block needs a caption. HTML provides a semantically correct way to group this content together.

lessons.title: The `<figure>` Element
lessons.content: The `<figure>` element represents self-contained content, like an image, illustration, or code snippet, that is referenced in the main text.

lessons.title: Wrap an image in a `<figure>` tag.

lessons.question: What kind of content is `<figure>` meant for?

lessons.title: The `<figcaption>` Element
lessons.content: The `<figcaption>` element represents a caption or legend for the content of its parent `<figure>` element.

lessons.title: Add a caption to an image inside a figure.

lessons.question: Where can a `<figcaption>` be placed inside a `<figure>`?
options: As the first or last child
lessons.correct: As the first or last child

lessons.title: Create a figure for a code block with a caption.
Caption Captain! 캡
lessons.content: You now know the professional, semantic way to associate captions with their content, improving meaning and accessibility.

lessons.title: More Than Just Keywords
lessons.content: The `<head>` section and its `<meta>` tags are powerful tools for controlling how your site appears on search engines and social media.

lessons.title: Controlling Search Engines
lessons.content: You can give instructions to search engine crawlers, for example, `<meta name='robots' content='noindex, nofollow'>` tells them not to index the page or follow its links.

lessons.title: Add a meta tag to tell search engines not to index a page.

lessons.question: What does `content='nofollow'` do?
options: Tells crawlers not to follow links on the page
lessons.correct: Tells crawlers not to follow links on the page

lessons.title: The Open Graph Protocol
lessons.content: The Open Graph protocol (used by Facebook, Twitter, etc.) lets you control how your content appears when shared. These are `<meta>` tags with `property` instead of `name`.

lessons.title: Essential OG Tags
lessons.content: Key Open Graph tags include `og:title`, `og:description`, `og:image`, and `og:url`.

lessons.title: Add an Open Graph title and description to your page.
lessons.expectedAnswer:
<meta property='og:title' content='My Awesome Article'>
<meta property='og:description' content='A summary of the article.'>
blocks:
<meta property='og:title' content='My Awesome Article'>
<meta property='og:description' content='A summary of the article.'>

lessons.title: Specify the preview image for social media sharing.

lessons.instruction: Add the `og:url` property for the page's canonical URL.

lessons.title: Social Sharer! 🔗
lessons.content: You can now control your site's appearance beyond your own domain, ensuring a professional look when shared across the web.

lessons.title: Graphics in HTML
lessons.content: Besides raster images (``), HTML supports two powerful ways to create graphics directly in the browser: SVG and Canvas.

lessons.title: SVG: Scalable Vector Graphics
lessons.content: SVG is an XML-based format for describing 2D graphics. It's resolution-independent, meaning it scales perfectly to any size without losing quality. Great for logos and icons.

lessons.title: Embed a simple SVG circle directly in your HTML.
lessons.expectedAnswer:
<svg width='100' height='100'>
  <circle cx='50' cy='50' r='40' fill='red' />
</svg>
blocks:
<svg width='100' height='100'>
  <circle cx='50' cy='50' r='40' fill='red' />
</svg>

lessons.question: What is the main advantage of SVG?

lessons.title: Canvas
lessons.content: The `<canvas>` element provides a drawing surface. You use JavaScript to draw on it pixel by pixel. It's a 'fire and forget' model, great for games and complex visualizations.

lessons.title: Create a canvas element with a specific width and height.

lessons.question: Which graphics technology relies heavily on JavaScript to draw?

lessons.title: SVG vs. Canvas
lessons.content: Use SVG for static, shape-based graphics that need to be sharp at all sizes. Use Canvas for dynamic, pixel-based graphics like games or real-time data charts.

lessons.question: Which would be better for an interactive game of Pong?

lessons.title: Graphics Guru! 🎨
lessons.content: You understand the fundamentals of the two main graphics technologies in HTML. This opens the door to creating rich visual experiences beyond standard text and images.

lessons.title: Writing Professional HTML
lessons.content: Let's review some best practices that distinguish clean, professional HTML from messy code.

lessons.title: Validate Your HTML
lessons.content: Always run your HTML through a validator, like the W3C Markup Validation Service. It helps catch errors and ensures your code is compliant.

lessons.question: Why should you validate your HTML?
options: To catch errors and ensure browser compatibility
lessons.correct: To catch errors and ensure browser compatibility

lessons.title: Use Lowercase Tags
lessons.content: While HTML isn't case-sensitive, the community standard is to always write tags and attributes in lowercase for consistency and readability.

lessons.question: Which is the preferred style?

lessons.title: Close All Tags
lessons.content:
While some tags are self-closing (``) and some browsers might render unclosed tags (`

`), you should always explicitly close your container tags (e.g., `

...

`).

lessons.title: Meaningful Structure
lessons.content: Structure your document logically with headings and semantic tags. Don't just use `<div>` for everything. A well-structured document is easier to maintain and better for A11y/SEO.

lessons.title: Indentation
lessons.content: Properly indent your nested elements. This doesn't change how the page looks, but it makes the code infinitely easier for humans to read and debug.

lessons.question: Does code indentation affect how the page is displayed?
options: No, it's only for human readability
lessons.correct: No, it's only for human readability

lessons.title: HTML Professional! 🏆
lessons.content: You not only know the tags, but you know how to write clean, valid, and maintainable HTML. This is the mark of a true professional.

lessons.title: Advanced HTML Review
lessons.content: You've gone far beyond the basics and learned the tools to create complex, accessible, and modern HTML documents. Let's test your knowledge.

To make a table cell span two columns, you use...
Which element provides multiple image sources for responsiveness?
The best tag for a site's main navigation menu is...
What is the primary purpose of ARIA attributes?
To create a native show/hide widget without JavaScript, you use...
Which meta tag property is used for social media sharing previews?

lessons.title: Ready for Anything
lessons.content: With your deep knowledge of HTML, you are now perfectly prepared to learn CSS and JavaScript to bring these well-structured documents to life.

lessons.title: HTML Master! 🏅
lessons.content: Congratulations! You have achieved a master's understanding of HTML. You are ready to build any web structure imaginable.
